title: Using passives
subtitle: It was believed that the plan would fail.
summary: Decide when a passive is the better choice: to leave out the agent, to keep the topic at the front, and to avoid a that-clause subject.

lesson.heading: Leaving out the agent
lesson.text: A passive lets us leave out the **agent** (the subject of the matching active sentence) by dropping the phrase with **by**. We prefer a passive when the agent is not known, is 'people in general', is unimportant, or is obvious.

examples.text: My office **was broken into** when I was on holiday.
An order form **can be found** on page 2.
He **is thought** to be somewhere in Russia.

examples.note: the agent is obvious - medical staff

lesson.heading: Factual writing
lesson.text: In factual writing - describing a procedure or a process - we often leave the agent out altogether and use one passive after another.

examples.text: Nuclear waste will still be radioactive even after 20,000 years, so it **must be disposed of** very carefully.
It **can be stored** as a liquid in stainless-steel containers which **are encased** in concrete.
The most dangerous nuclear waste **can be turned** into glass which **will be stored** in deep underground mines.

left.label: Informal: an active with a vague subject
left.text: people, somebody / someone, something, they, we, you - even when we don't know who the agent is
examples: They're installing the new computer system next month.

right.label: Formal: a passive with no agent
right.text: the mention of an agent is avoided completely
examples: The new computer system is being installed next month.

lesson.heading: A related noun as the subject
lesson.text: Some verbs have a related noun with the same meaning. That noun can become the subject of a passive sentence, with a new passive verb introduced.

examples.text: The new computer system is being installed next month. - **The installation** of the new computer system **will be completed** by next month.
They will consider the issue at next week's meeting. - **Consideration will be given** to the issue at next week's meeting.

lesson.heading: Topic first, comment last
lesson.text: English usually puts the **topic** (what we are already talking about) at the start of a clause and the **comment** on it at the end. A passive often lets us do this - and it lets us move a long subject to the end.

examples.text: The three machines tested for the report contained different types of safety valve. **All the valves were manufactured** by the Boron Group in Germany.
examples.note: the valves are the topic, so they come first

examples.text: **I was surprised by** Dev's decision to give up his job and move to Sydney.
examples.note: more natural than 'Dev's decision to give up his job and move to Sydney surprised me'

lesson.heading: it + passive instead of a that-clause subject
lesson.text: Rather than making a **that**-clause the subject of a passive sentence, it is normal to start with **it**.

examples.text: Everybody believed (that) the plan would fail.
**It was believed that** the plan would fail.
That the plan would fail was believed by everybody.

lesson.text: If naming the agent adds nothing - or if it would push a long phrase to the front of your sentence - the passive is almost always the better choice.

exercises.prompt: They built the main stadium in under three years. - The main stadium ___ in under three years.
exercises.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle.

exercises.prompt: They are holding the rowing competition on the River Nene. - The rowing competition ___ on the River Nene.
exercises.explanation: Present continuous passive: is being + past participle.

exercises.prompt: They will take down the temporary stands after the Games. - The temporary stands ___ after the Games.
exercises.explanation: will + be + past participle; the particle down stays with the verb.

exercises.prompt: Why is a passive the natural choice in each sentence?
categories: The agent is unknown or unimportant
The agent is obvious or 'people in general'

items.text: My office was broken into when I was on holiday.
An order form can be found on page 2.
He is thought to be somewhere in Russia.
She is being treated in hospital.

exercises.prompt: They were using the handball venue as a warehouse until a year ago. - The handball venue ___ as a warehouse until a year ago.
exercises.explanation: Past continuous passive: was being + past participle.

exercises.prompt: They should have finished the badminton arena by now. - The badminton arena ___ by now.
exercises.explanation: The passive of should have + past participle is should have been + past participle.

exercises.statement: I was surprised by Dev's decision to give up his job and move to Sydney.
exercises.explanation: Correct - and more natural than the active, because the passive keeps the long subject at the end.

exercises.prompt: They will appoint a new managing director next week. - The ___ of a new managing director will be made next week.
exercises.explanation: A related noun can become the subject of a passive: the appointment ... will be made.

exercises.prompt: They demolished the building in only two days. - The ___ of the building was completed in only two days.
exercises.explanation: demolish gives the noun demolition, which takes the new passive verb was completed.

exercises.prompt: It ___ that there will be a 38-55 cm rise in average sea levels by the year 2100.
exercises.explanation: it + passive verb + that-clause reports a figure without naming who worked it out.

exercises.statement: That the plan would fail was believed by everybody.
exercises.explanation: It was believed that the plan would fail. We start with it rather than making the that-clause the subject.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'They will consider the issue at next week's meeting', starting with a noun formed from consider.
exercises.answer: Consideration will be given to the issue at next week's meeting
exercises.explanation: The related noun consideration becomes the subject, with the new passive verb be given.
